displayQuote: Be patient and tough; some day this pain will be useful to you

meta.title: Who really said "Be patient and tough; some day this pain will be useful to you"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Ovid really wrote it — Amores 3.11, line 7: "Perfer et obdura! dolor hic tibi proderit olim." But the familiar English is a loose, uncredited modern rendering.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Be patient and tough; some day this pain will be useful to you'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Ovid — Amores 3.11a.7, confirmed in two Latin editions. But it's a breakup pep talk he abandons 32 lines later, and the English wording has no credited translator.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 20 March 43 BC – AD 17/18 · Roman poet of the Amores, Ars Amatoria & Tristia
answer.sourceLine: Ovid really did write this line. It is Amores Book 3, Elegy 11a, line 7 — “Perfer et obdura! dolor hic tibi proderit olim” — confirmed in two independent scholarly Latin texts. The catch is the English: the familiar “Be patient and tough” wording is a loose modern rendering with no translator credited anywhere I could find, and the standard 1914 Loeb translation words it quite differently.

source.heading: The source: Amores 3.11a, line 7

docMeta.dd: “Perfer et obdura! dolor hic tibi proderit olim”
16 BC, in five books; later revised by Ovid into the surviving three
Popular English wording — no translator credited. Loeb (Showerman, 1914): “Persist, and endure! this smart will some day bring thee good.”

source.excerpt:
Vicimus et domitum pedibus calcamus amorem;
    venerunt capiti cornua sera meo.
Perfer et obdura! dolor hic tibi proderit olim;
    saepe tulit lassis sucus amarus opem.
trail: The line sits at Amores 3.11a, line 7 in the critical Latin text of R. Ehwald (Teubner, 1907), hosted by Perseus ↗: “Perfer et obdura! dolor hic tibi proderit olim.”
The Latin Library’s text of Amores III ↗ carries the identical line in the same position — an independent confirmation of the wording.

The 1914 bilingual edition translated by Grant Showerman ↗ prints the Latin (p. 488) opposite his English (p. 489), which reads “Persist, and endure! this smart will some day bring thee good” — showing the popular wording is not the standard translation.
Neither Quote Investigator nor the Wikiquote page for Ovid ↗ carries an entry for this line, so the attribution here rests on the Latin texts directly rather than on prior quote research.
source.excerptNote: Lines 5–8 of the elegy. Grant Showerman’s 1914 English renders them: “Victory is mine, and I tread under foot my conquered love; courage has entered my heart, though late. Persist, and endure! this smart will some day bring thee good; oft has bitter potion brought help to the languishing.” The bitter-medicine image in the fourth line is the point — the pain is framed as a purgative for love, not as life advice.

source.rightsNote: Ovid’s Latin has been in the public domain for centuries, and Grant Showerman’s 1914 English translation is public domain in the United States as a pre-1931 publication. But rights on a translated quotation attach to the exact English shown, and the wording displayed here matches no translation I could identify — no translator, edition, or first-publication date is credited by any source that circulates it. Because its origin is unknown, no public-domain status is asserted for this specific English phrasing. Anyone needing a clearly free English text should quote Showerman’s 1914 rendering, or the Latin itself.

author.name: Ovid
author.heading: Who was Ovid?
author.metaLine: 20 March 43 BC – AD 17/18 · Roman poet, born Publius Ovidius Naso
author.bio: Publius Ovidius Naso was a Roman poet of the Augustan age, best known for the Metamorphoses, the Ars Amatoria and the Amores — the three-book collection of love elegies in which this line appears. The imperative perfer et obdura (“bear it and hold firm”) was something of a personal refrain for him: it turns up as courtship advice in Ars Amatoria 2.178, and again in the Tristia, written after, as he puts it there, the emperor’s anger tore him away. Only in the Amores, though, is it followed by the clause that made the quote famous.

misattribution.heading: The author is right. Two other things aren’t.
misattribution.intro: This is an unusual case for a viral classical quote: the attribution actually holds up. Ovid wrote the line, and it can be pinned to a single verse. What travels badly is the English wording and the situation the line belongs to.

items.why: No translator is named for “Be patient and tough; some day this pain will be useful to you” in any source I could locate. The standard published English differs markedly: Grant Showerman’s 1914 Loeb translation gives “Persist, and endure! this smart will some day bring thee good” (1914 edition, p. 489 ↗). Treat the popular phrasing as a paraphrase, not as Ovid’s translated words.

Quoted alone it reads as universal advice about hardship. In place it is one man’s self-administered pep talk in a poem about quitting a destructive affair — and it does not work. Later in the same elegy he concedes “love, I think, is winning” and that he can live neither with her nor without her (Amores 3.11 ↗).

Many readers encounter the sentiment as the title of the novel Someday This Pain Will Be Useful to You, published in 2007 by Frances Foster Books. The title alludes to Ovid’s line rather than originating it (Wikipedia ↗).

Quote sites routinely credit this to Ovid with no reference. It has a precise address — Amores 3.11a, line 7 — and the same two-word imperative appears elsewhere in his work with a different ending, so naming the work matters (Ars Amatoria 2.178 ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Ovid wrote it, at Amores 3.11a, line 7 ↗ — but as a man bracing himself for a breakup he is about to lose, and in words no named translator has ever claimed.

context.heading: A pep talk that fails 32 lines later
lead: Amores 3.11 is not a poem of consolation. It is a breakup poem, and the man being addressed is the poet himself. He opens by announcing that he has finally broken free — “Much have I endured, and for long time… withdraw from my tired-out breast, base love!” — and then, at line 7, braces himself for the withdrawal: bear it, hold firm, this hurt will pay off eventually.

It does not pay off. Later in the same poem (line 39) the resolve collapses completely: sic ego nec sine te nec tecum vivere possum — I can live neither with you nor without you. In the lines just before it he admits that love and hate are fighting over his “fickle heart” and that “love, I think, is winning.” The motivational poster keeps line 7 and quietly drops the ending.
context.detailsSummary: Where else Ovid uses the phrase
detailsBody: The two-word command perfer et obdura appears at least three times across Ovid’s career, each time meaning something different. In Ars Amatoria 2.177–78 it is tactical dating advice: if she is not kind to you, “Perfer et obdura: postmodo mitis erit” — endure, and later she will soften.

In Tristia 5.11 it is addressed to his wife amid his banishment: “Perfer et obdura; multo graviora tulisti, / eripuit cum me principis ira tibi” — bear it and hold firm; you have borne far worse, when the prince’s anger snatched me from you.

Only the Amores instance carries the second half — dolor hic tibi proderit olim — which is the clause the modern quotation actually depends on. So while the imperative is vintage Ovid, the specific sentence people quote lives at exactly one address.
context.pull: The line is Ovid talking himself out of a relationship — and losing the argument.

sourcesVerified.claim: Ovid's Amores 3.11a, line 7 reads "Perfer et obdura! dolor hic tibi proderit olim" in the Ehwald (Teubner, 1907) critical Latin text.

An independent Latin text of Amores Book III contains the same line at Elegy XI, line 7, with the surrounding lines "vicimus et domitum pedibus calcamus amorem" and "saepe tulit lassis sucus amarus opem".

The 1914 bilingual edition of Heroides and Amores was translated by Grant Showerman (1870-1935), published London: W. Heinemann / New York: Macmillan, 1914; its text renders the line "Persist, and endure! this smart will some day bring thee good" on the page facing the Latin.
Ovid reuses "Perfer et obdura" at Ars Amatoria 2.178 ("Perfer et obdura: postmodo mitis erit"), and the clause "dolor hic tibi proderit olim" does NOT appear in that book.
Ovid reuses "Perfer et obdura" in Tristia Book 5, Poem 11 ("Perfer et obdura; multo grauiora tulisti, / eripuit cum me principis ira tibi"), and "dolor hic tibi proderit olim" does not appear there.

The Amores was first published in 16 BC in five books, and Ovid later edited it down into the three-book edition that survives; Amores 3.11a is the speaker declaring he has freed himself, and 3.11b is his reversal.
Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso) lived 20 March 43 BC to AD 17/18 and was a Roman poet during the reign of Augustus; his works include the Amores, Ars Amatoria and Tristia.

Peter Cameron's novel Someday This Pain Will Be Useful to You was published in 2007 by Frances Foster Books, and its title alludes to a line from Ovid's Amores, "Perfer et obdura, dolor hic tibi proderit olim."
Wikiquote's page for Ovid contains no entry for "Perfer et obdura", "proderit olim", or "this pain will be useful" in any section.
